prompt.context: Action Med received many pharma products in clinical development as a result of a recent acquisition, including a drug called BPL to treat resistant HIV. The total cost of drug development is $2 billion USD (includes R&D and anticipated marketing spend). Patients have resistant HIV when combination therapy fails to achieve complete viral suppression (virological failure). BPL treats patients who have virological failure after taking 3+ medications.
prompt.question: Action Med wants to know the target patient population for this product and how many patients will realistically take the drug. They also need to focus their marketing efforts on specific healthcare sites. How would you begin to think about this problem?

clarifying_info.q: What defines resistant HIV for this case?
clarifying_info.a: Patients have resistant HIV when combination therapy fails to achieve complete viral suppression (virological failure). BPL treats patients who have virological failure after taking 3+ medications.

clarifying_info.q: What types of healthcare facilities are we considering?
clarifying_info.a: Private hospitals, Academic Centers of Excellence, and small private practices.

clarifying_info.q: Do we need to consider growth rates or time value of money?
clarifying_info.a: No — assume no growth rate and that time value of money is not an issue. You can multiply 1 year of revenue by 5 to get 5-year revenue.

clarifying_info.q: Can Action Med target multiple types of healthcare providers?
clarifying_info.a: No — they only have the marketing resources to target 1 type of healthcare provider at this time.

exhibits.title: Healthcare Facility Data for BPL Market Sizing
exhibits.shows: A table with four types of healthcare facilities (Private Hospital, Academic Center of Excellence, Small Private Practice) and columns for: number of facilities in the US, average patients per hospital with HIV, % of patients with resistant HIV, potential uptake of BPL among resistant HIV patients, number of pills per patient per year, and price per pack of 6 pills.

exhibits.title: Pharma Product Sales Mix and Neurology Market Share 2018–2022
exhibits.shows: A pie chart showing 2018 pharma product sales split by therapeutic area (Cardiovascular 38%, Neurology 20%, Oncology 42%), and a bar chart showing neurology market share in 2018 vs. 2022 for Pfizer, AstraZeneca, GSK, and Sanofi. Additional notes state total patients buying prescription medication = 200M, Action Med provides 70% of Sanofi's APIs in both 2018 and projected to 2022, and average price of Action Med API sold to Sanofi = $75.

framework: Market sizing: quantify the total addressable patient population (total HIV patients → resistant HIV patients → patients who will actually take BPL by uptake rate)
Revenue potential by channel: calculate annual and 5-year revenue per healthcare facility type to identify the highest-value segment to target
Competitive environment: assess existing HIV therapies, pipeline drugs, and market dynamics that affect BPL uptake
Pricing strategy: determine appropriate price per course of treatment given R&D cost and competitive positioning
Cost recovery analysis: evaluate whether projected revenues across all business lines will recover the $2B development investment
Go-to-market focus: identify which healthcare site type (private hospital, academic center, private practice) to prioritize with limited marketing resources

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, calculate annual revenue and 5-year revenue for each type of healthcare facility. Which type should Action Med target?
questions.guidance: A strong candidate sets up the revenue formula: (number of facilities) × (avg HIV patients) × (% resistant HIV) × (uptake %) × (pills per patient per year ÷ pills per pack) × (price per pack). They calculate all three facility types, compare 5-year revenues, and recommend Academic Centers of Excellence as the highest-revenue segment. An excellent candidate also explains why each multiplier matters and notes that Academic Centers have the largest absolute number of resistant HIV patients per facility.

math.setup: Revenue per facility type = (# facilities) × (avg HIV patients/facility) × (% resistant HIV) × (uptake %) × (24 pills/year ÷ 6 pills/pack) × ($100/pack)
math.answer: Academic Centers of Excellence generate the highest 5-year revenue at $1.152B. Action Med should target Academic Centers of Excellence.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, calculate the additional API revenue Action Med will earn from Sanofi's predicted increase in neurology market share by 2022 compared to 2018.
questions.guidance: A strong candidate identifies that Sanofi's neurology market share grows from 10% to 40% in the chart, then chains the multipliers: total prescription patients × neurology share of pharma sales × Sanofi 2022 market share × Action Med API share × price per patient. They isolate only the 2022 figure since Prompt 2 asks for the 2022 revenue level (not an incremental change from 2018 per the calculation guidance). An excellent candidate explicitly states the assumption that market size is constant and explains each step.

math.setup: Action Med API revenue from Sanofi in 2022 = (total prescription patients) × (% in neurology) × (Sanofi 2022 market share) × (Action Med API share) × (price per patient/year)
steps: Revenue: 11.2M × $75 = $840M (note: casebook states $848M — treat as $840M or $848M depending on rounding; casebook answer is $848M)
math.answer: Approximately $840M–$848M in API revenue from Sanofi in 2022.

questions.prompt: Combining the 5-year BPL revenue from Academic Centers of Excellence and the 2022 API revenue from Sanofi, will Action Med recover its $2B R&D and marketing investment?
questions.guidance: A strong candidate adds $1.152B (5-year BPL revenue) + $848M (Sanofi API revenue in 2022) = ~$2.0B, concluding that Action Med will just barely cover its $2B investment. An excellent candidate notes this is not a blockbuster outcome — the drug essentially breaks even — and flags risks such as slower uptake, competitive threats, or pricing pressure that could jeopardize cost recovery.

math.setup: Total combined revenue = 5-year BPL revenue (Academic Centers) + Sanofi API revenue in 2022
math.answer: Yes — combined revenue of ~$2.0B exactly covers the $2B investment, but there is no significant margin of safety.

recommendation: Action Med should target Academic Centers of Excellence for BPL marketing, as they generate the highest 5-year revenue of $1.152B among the three facility types.
When combined with projected Sanofi API revenue of ~$848M in 2022, Action Med will recover approximately $2.0B in total revenue, matching the $2B development cost.
risks: BPL is not a blockbuster drug — projected revenues only break even with development costs, leaving no cushion for delays, lower-than-expected uptake, or cost overruns.
Sanofi's market share projection of 40% in 2022 may not materialize if competitive dynamics shift.
The uptake assumption (20% for Academic Centers) could be optimistic if physicians are reluctant to prescribe a new resistant HIV therapy.
Action Med has limited marketing resources focused on a single provider type, increasing concentration risk.
next_steps: Validate patient uptake assumptions with key opinion leaders at Academic Centers of Excellence.
Conduct competitive landscape analysis to assess pipeline drugs for resistant HIV.
Explore whether marketing resources can be expanded to target a second provider type in later years to improve revenue upside.
Stress-test financial projections under lower uptake scenarios to confirm acceptable risk tolerance.
